title: How the Whole Story Fits
subtitle: Four faithful ways Christians read the Bible as one story that ends at Christ. And what hangs on the differences.
triageNote: That the Bible is one unfolding story climaxing in Christ is shared ground across every framework on this page. How the covenants connect, and how the place of Israel relates to the church, is a framework difference. It shapes whole traditions. We treat it as second-order. It is not a test of who belongs to Christ. It is a question that changes how you read almost every page after Genesis 3.
question: Is the Bible one story or many? And if it is one story, what holds the pieces together as it moves from Adam to Abraham to Moses to David to Jesus and finally to the church? When God made promises to Israel about land and offspring and blessing, are those promises fulfilled in the church, still owed to national Israel, or somehow both? The frameworks below are not four religions. They are four ways of answering one question. How does the whole story fit?
whyItMatters:
If you are new to the Bible, this can feel like an argument for specialists. It is not. How you read the whole story decides how you read every part of it.

Start with biblical theology. It simply means reading the Bible as a single developing story rather than a flat book of disconnected rules and verses. Once you decide the Bible is one story, you have to decide what shape that story has. And that shape determines four very practical things.

It decides what you do with the Old Testament law. When you read a command in Leviticus, is it still speaking to you, fulfilled and set aside, or somewhere in between. It decides how you think about Israel. When you read God's promises to the descendants of Abraham, do you, a Gentile believer in Christ, inherit those promises, or do they still belong to a national people. It decides how you understand baptism, because whether the church is a fresh continuation of Israel or a new thing entirely shapes whether the children of believers are included in the covenant sign the way Israelite children were. And it decides what you do with the sabbath, the weekly day of rest commanded at Sinai, because whether the Mosaic law still binds you determines whether Saturday or Sunday rest is a command or a freedom.

Four readers can love the same Jesus and read the same Bible and land in four different places on all four questions. That is what makes this worth understanding rather than ignoring.

positions.name: Covenant Theology
positions.inOneLine: The Bible is held together by a few overarching covenants, the church is the continuation of the one people of God begun with Israel, and every promise finds its yes in Christ.
positions.bestCase:
Let me tell you how I read the whole Bible, because once you see it you cannot unsee it. A covenant is a binding relationship that God establishes, with promises, obligations, and a sign. The whole of Scripture, I believe, runs on a small number of these covenants, and they fit inside each other like rings of a tree.

Before the fall, God related to Adam under what I call the covenant of works. The arrangement was simple. Perfect obedience, and you live. Adam failed, and we all fell with him. After the fall, God did not abandon us to that broken arrangement. He opened the covenant of grace, the single saving relationship that runs from the promise in Genesis 3 through Abraham, Moses, and David, all the way to the cross and to us. Every saint in every age has been saved the same way, by grace through faith in the Christ who was promised and then came. The administration changed across the ages. The substance never did.

This is why I read the Old Testament as my own family history and not as someone else's. When God told Abraham in Genesis 17 that he would be God to Abraham and to his children after him, he was describing the very promise I now live inside. The church does not replace Israel. The church is Israel, grown up and opened to the nations, the same olive tree of Romans 11 into which I, a wild branch, have been grafted. I use the word typology here. It means an earlier person or event or institution that God designed to point forward to a greater reality in Christ. Adam was a type of Christ. The Passover lamb was a type. The temple was a type. The story was always pointing somewhere.

And this is why I baptize my children. The sign of the covenant of grace once was circumcision, given to believers and their children alike. The covenant did not shrink when Christ came. It widened. So the children of believers still receive the sign, now baptism, as members of the covenant community awaiting their own faith. To cut them out would be to make the new covenant narrower than the old, and I cannot believe that grace contracted at the coming of Christ.

When people accuse covenant theology of erasing Israel, I want to be careful. I do not teach that God is finished with the Jewish people. I teach that there has only ever been one people of God. In Christ the dividing wall is down. That is not replacement. That is fulfillment.
advocates: The Westminster divines (Westminster Confession of Faith, 1646)

positions.name: Dispensationalism
positions.inOneLine: God works through distinct eras, Israel and the church remain distinct peoples, and many promises made to national Israel are still to be fulfilled to Israel literally.
positions.bestCase:
I read the Bible by paying close attention to who God is speaking to. And when. A dispensation is a distinct era in which God administers his dealings with humanity in a particular way, with its own arrangement and its own test. There is the innocence of Eden, the era after the fall, the era under the Mosaic law, the present era of the church, and the coming kingdom. God does not change. But the way he orders his house changes from age to age.

The heart of how I read Scripture is this. When God makes a promise, I want to let that promise mean what its first hearers would have understood it to mean. God told Abraham in Genesis 15 that his offspring would possess a specific land between specific rivers. Abraham did not hear a metaphor for the church. He heard a promise about land. The prophets describe Israel restored, the temple rebuilt, the nations streaming to Jerusalem. I take that seriously as a future for the actual people of Israel. I do not think those promises quietly transferred to the church and emptied of their original meaning.

So I hold that Israel and the church are distinct. The church is something genuinely new, born at Pentecost in Acts 2, a people of Jew and Gentile together in Christ. But the existence of the church does not cancel God's outstanding commitments to Israel as a nation. Romans 11 is my anchor here. Paul insists that God has not rejected his people, that their hardening is partial and temporary, and that all Israel will be saved. I read that as a real future for ethnic Israel, not as a poetic way of describing the church.

Not all of us read every detail the same way. I should be honest that there is a spectrum. The classic position drew very sharp lines between Israel and the church and between the law and grace. Progressive dispensationalists, and I count myself among those who have learned from them, see far more continuity. We hold that the kingdom Christ brings is already inaugurated and that the new covenant is already at work in the church, even while we still expect promises to Israel to find a literal fulfillment. We are not waiting for two unrelated stories to end. We are watching one story unfold in stages we refuse to collapse prematurely.

Why does this matter pastorally. Because I read my Bible expecting God to keep his word in the exact terms he gave it. If he can promise a land to Abraham and then dissolve that promise into something else entirely, I lose confidence that the promises he makes to me will mean what they say either. God's faithfulness to Israel is, for me, the proof. His word does not bend.
advocates: Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock (progressive dispensationalism)

positions.name: Progressive Covenantalism
positions.inOneLine: Trace the biblical covenants as they progress and climax in Christ and the new covenant, and you find one people of God in Christ, without the works-grace scaffolding of classic covenant theology.
positions.bestCase:
I want to read the Bible the way it actually presents itself, covenant by covenant, watching each one build on the last until they all arrive at Christ. So I do not start with a grand structure of two covenants and then fit the Bible into it. I start with the covenants Scripture names out loud. The covenant with Noah, the Abrahamic covenant, the Mosaic covenant, the covenant with David, and then the new covenant. I trace how each one advances the story and how each one finds its goal in Jesus.

When I follow that progression, here is what I see. The Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 12, 15, and 17 makes promises of offspring, land, and worldwide blessing. The Mosaic covenant, the arrangement God made with the nation of Israel at Sinai, governs that people for a season but was never the destination. It was, as Galatians 3 says, a guardian until Christ came. The new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 is the climax, the relationship in which God writes his law on hearts and forgives sins fully through Christ.

This puts me between the other two views, and I think that is exactly where the text puts me. With covenant theology, I hold that there is one people of God and that the church is its fulfillment, not a parenthesis. Galatians 3:29 is plain. If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to the promise. I do not expect a separate future program for national Israel as a distinct people, because I believe the promises to Abraham land on Christ first, the true offspring, and then on everyone united to him, Jew and Gentile alike.

But I part with classic covenant theology on its framing. I do not build my system on a covenant of works and a single covenant of grace stretched over all of history. I find those categories more imposed than discovered. The covenants are not all the same covenant in different clothes. They genuinely progress, and some of them, like the Mosaic, were always temporary by design. This matters most for baptism. Because I see the new covenant as a community of those who actually know the Lord, from the least to the greatest as Jeremiah says, I baptize believers, not infants. The new covenant community is not a mixed nation. It is the gathered people who have come to faith.

Typology is the engine of how I read. Israel, the temple, the priesthood, the land, all of them were patterns God built to point to Christ and the new creation. So I do not flatten them into the church mechanically, and I do not leave them hanging as unfulfilled promises to a nation. I follow them to Jesus, where they were always headed.
advocates: Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum (Kingdom through Covenant)
Stephen Wellum and Brent Parker (Covenantal and Dispensational Theologies, eds.)

positions.name: New Covenant Theology
positions.inOneLine: The law of Moses came as a single unit and has been fulfilled and replaced by the law of Christ, so the Mosaic covenant, including the sabbath, does not directly bind the Christian.
positions.bestCase:
I read the Bible asking one sharp question. What is my relationship, as a Christian, to the law God gave at Sinai. And my answer is that the law of Moses came to Israel as a whole, a single covenant package, and that whole package has reached its end in Christ.

Let me be careful, because this is easy to misunderstand. I am not saying the Old Testament does not matter or that God's moral character changed. I am saying that the Mosaic covenant was a unit. People often slice it into moral, civil, and ceremonial parts and then keep the moral part while discarding the rest. I do not find that division in the text. The law was given as one covenant to one nation for one era, and when Christ came, he fulfilled all of it and brought it to its appointed end.

In its place I am given the law of Christ, the phrase Paul uses in Galatians. This is the will of God as it comes to me now, through Christ and his apostles, the teaching of Jesus and the shape of the new covenant ethic. Much of it overlaps with the old commands, because God's righteousness is consistent. Nine of the Ten Commandments are repeated and even deepened in the New Testament. But they bind me as the law of Christ, not as the covenant of Sinai.

The one that is not repeated as a command is the sabbath. And that is the test case that shows what my view actually changes. I do not believe the weekly sabbath, the Saturday rest commanded at Sinai, is binding on the Christian as law. Hebrews treats the sabbath as a shadow whose substance is the rest we have in Christ. So I gather with the church on the Lord's Day with joy, but I do not bind anyone's conscience to a day, because Colossians 2 tells me not to let anyone judge me regarding a sabbath. The shadow has met its reality.

Matthew 5:17 is where people push back hardest, where Jesus says he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it. I take that word fulfill with full weight. He did not discard the law. He brought it to its goal and completion, the way a promise is fulfilled when it comes true. After that, you do not keep going back to the promise as though it were still waiting. You live in light of the One who fulfilled it. That is how I read the whole Bible. The law was real, it was good, and it was always pointing to Christ, who is now my Lord and my law.
advocates: Tom Wells and Fred Zaspel (New Covenant Theology)
Douglas Moo (in part, on the law)

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared foundation, read differently by each
biblicalEvidence.summary: God promises Abraham offspring, a land, and blessing to all nations through him, and formally cuts a covenant to seal it. This is the seedbed of every framework, because every later covenant grows out of these promises. The Abrahamic covenant is the binding relationship in which God commits himself to Abraham and his descendants with land, offspring, and worldwide blessing.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It pulls in two directions at once, which is hard for any view that wants it simple. The promise of worldwide blessing reaches past Israel to the nations, yet the promise of a specific land is given in concrete geographic terms.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Covenant theology and progressive covenantalism stress the offspring and blessing promises as fulfilled in Christ and his multinational people, reading the land as a type of the renewed creation believers inherit. Dispensationalism stresses that the land promise was given in literal terms and has never been fully realized, so it still awaits fulfillment for national Israel. New covenant theology reads the Abrahamic promise as fulfilled in Christ and the gospel going to the nations, the land swallowed up in the new creation.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Progressive covenantalism and new covenant theology
biblicalEvidence.summary: God promises a new covenant, not like the one made at the exodus that Israel broke. In it he writes his law on hearts, is their God, and forgives their sins, so that all of them, from the least to the greatest, will know him. The new covenant is the climactic saving relationship God establishes through Christ, marked by inward transformation and full forgiveness.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for covenant theology's case for infant baptism. If the defining mark of the new covenant is that all its members truly know the Lord, it is difficult to argue that the covenant community should still include those who do not yet believe.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Covenant theology answers that the new covenant is administered through a community that remains mixed in this age, just as Israel was, so the sign still belongs to households. Progressive covenantalism and new covenant theology read it as describing a community of actual believers, which grounds believer's baptism. Dispensationalism notes the new covenant is explicitly made with the house of Israel and Judah, and reads it as having an application to the church now and a fuller realization for Israel later.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul argues the law, added 430 years after the promise to Abraham, cannot annul that promise. The law was a guardian until Christ. Now, in Christ, there is neither Jew nor Greek, and those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to the promise.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for dispensationalism. The text says believers in Christ, including Gentiles, are Abraham's offspring and heirs of the promise, which presses against a sharp permanent distinction between Israel and the church.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Covenant theology and progressive covenantalism take this as decisive proof that the one people of God is united in Christ and that Gentile believers inherit Abraham's promises directly. Dispensationalism responds that being Abraham's spiritual offspring for salvation does not erase God's separate national promises, and that this passage concerns how anyone is justified, not whether Israel has a future. New covenant theology reads the guardian language as confirming the Mosaic law had a fixed term that has ended.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Dispensationalism (and a real tension for the others)
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul insists God has not rejected his people Israel. Their hardening is partial and temporary. Gentiles are wild branches grafted into the cultivated olive tree, and natural branches can be grafted back in. He concludes that all Israel will be saved.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for any view that fully merges Israel into the church with no remaining future, because Paul clearly expects something still to come for ethnic Israel.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Dispensationalism reads this as a plain promise of future restoration for national Israel. Covenant theology reads the one olive tree as proof of a single people of God, and reads all Israel will be saved as the full number of elect Jews gathered across history, or a large turning of Jewish people to Christ, without a separate national program. Progressive covenantalism reads it similarly, as a future ingathering of Jewish people into the one body in Christ. New covenant theology lands near covenant theology here.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: New covenant theology and progressive covenantalism
biblicalEvidence.summary: Quoting Jeremiah 31 at length, the writer says that in speaking of a new covenant, God makes the first one obsolete, and what is obsolete is ready to vanish away. The new covenant is founded on better promises and a better priest.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for the classic covenant-theology framing of one unbroken covenant of grace with merely changing administrations, since the text speaks of a first covenant becoming obsolete and being replaced.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: New covenant theology takes this as direct support that the Mosaic covenant is finished and replaced. Progressive covenantalism agrees the Mosaic covenant is obsolete while holding the new covenant fulfills the Abrahamic promise. Covenant theology clarifies that what becomes obsolete is the old Mosaic administration, not the underlying covenant of grace, which it says continues and deepens. Dispensationalism reads the contrast as real and significant while still expecting Israel's share in the new covenant.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: A test for every view, especially new covenant theology
biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus says he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them, that not the smallest stroke will pass until all is accomplished, and that those who relax the least command and teach others to do so will be called least in the kingdom.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for new covenant theology, because Jesus seems to uphold the abiding authority of the commands, which sits awkwardly with the claim that the Mosaic law as a whole has been set aside.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: New covenant theology leans on the word fulfill, arguing Jesus brings the law to its goal and completion so it now reaches us transformed as the law of Christ, not abolished but also not directly binding in its old form. Covenant theology reads it as Christ upholding the enduring moral law. Progressive covenantalism reads fulfill through typology, the law reaching its intended target in Christ. Dispensationalism notes the phrase until all is accomplished, leaving room for the law's role across the eras.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, with a sharp split on verse 39
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Spirit is poured out, the church is born, and Peter preaches that the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord calls. He calls his hearers to repent and be baptized.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: The phrase for you and for your children is hard for credobaptist views (believer's baptism only), while the call to repent and be baptized in response to the word is pressed by those same views against infant baptism.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Covenant theology hears for your children as continuity with the household pattern of the Abrahamic covenant, supporting infant baptism. Progressive covenantalism and new covenant theology read for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord calls as defining the promise by God's calling and personal response, supporting believer's baptism. Dispensationalism reads Pentecost as the distinct birth of the church, a new work alongside God's ongoing plan for Israel.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul says let no one pass judgment on you regarding food and drink, a festival, a new moon, or a sabbath, for these are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for views that keep the weekly sabbath as a binding creation ordinance, since Paul lists the sabbath among shadows fulfilled in Christ.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: New covenant theology reads this as direct evidence that the sabbath command is fulfilled and no longer binds the conscience. Covenant theology distinguishes the ceremonial sabbaths of the festal calendar from the weekly creation sabbath, arguing only the former are in view here. Progressive covenantalism tends toward the new covenant theology reading. Dispensationalism agrees the sabbath was tied to the Mosaic era and is not imposed on the church.

weighing:
What follows is my judgment, offered tentatively and held loosely. I write it so you know a real person stands behind these words, not so you will simply adopt it.

My own reading leans toward seeing one people of God who find their identity in Christ, with the church as the fulfillment of the promises to Abraham rather than a separate track. Galatians 3:29 is hard to read any other way. Belong to Christ, and you are Abraham's offspring. That single sentence does more to settle my mind than any system. And yet Romans 11 will not let me close the book on national Israel as cleanly as I might like. Paul plainly expects something. The honest position holds both, a single people in Christ and a real future ingathering, even when the seams show.

On the law, I find the new covenant theology instinct clarifying, that the Mosaic covenant came as a unit and reached its goal in Christ, and I am not as confident as classic covenant theology that the threefold division of the law is given to us in the text rather than read into it. But I also notice how relentlessly Jesus intensifies the commands in Matthew 5, and I am wary of any view that makes the Old Testament feel like a closed chapter rather than my own Scripture.

What I am most sure of is the smallest claim and the largest one at the same time. The Bible is one story, and it ends at Christ. Every framework on this page confesses that. The disagreements are about the wiring underneath a shared and glorious conviction. I would rather sit under a faithful teacher from any of these four traditions than under no teacher who reads the whole story at all.
charitableDisagreement:
It is worth naming the ugly thing these views are usually accused of, supersessionism, which is the belief that the church has simply replaced Israel so that God is finished with the Jewish people and their election is revoked. In its hard form, the form that fed centuries of contempt and worse, every framework on this page rejects it. Covenant theology and progressive covenantalism do not teach that God discarded the Jews, they teach that Jew and Gentile are made one in Christ. Dispensationalism is the strongest guardian against any erasure of Israel. New covenant theology affirms God's ongoing mercy to Jewish people. None of these is the old replacement theology that did such harm, and it is a slander to treat them as if they were.

So is this a hill to die on. No. It is a hill to study on, to think hard on, even to argue on with people you love and respect. Where you land will shape your church, your baptism, your reading of the Old Testament, and your sense of God's plan, and those are not small. But a Christian who reads the Bible through any of these four frameworks is a brother or sister reading the same story toward the same Christ. Hold your view with conviction. Hold your neighbor's with honor. And do not confuse the wiring of the house with the foundation, which is one for all of us.

relatedDebates.note: This flows almost directly from the frameworks. If the church continues the one covenant community begun with Israel and its households, as covenant theology holds, the sign goes to believers and their children. If the new covenant community is defined by those who actually know the Lord, as progressive covenantalism and new covenant theology hold, the sign goes to professing believers only. The water question is downstream of the whole-story question.

relatedDebates.topic: The place of national Israel and the modern state
relatedDebates.note: Whether God still owes literal promises to national Israel shapes how some Christians read current events in the Middle East. Dispensationalism has historically connected the regathering of Jewish people to the land with prophecy. The other frameworks generally caution against reading the modern state directly off the biblical promises, since they see those promises fulfilled in Christ. This is a place where theology and politics get tangled and where care is needed.

relatedDebates.topic: Continuity versus discontinuity in the law
relatedDebates.note: Everything here can be plotted on a single line. How much of the Mosaic law carries straight into the Christian life. Covenant theology sits toward continuity, keeping the moral law and the weekly sabbath. New covenant theology sits toward discontinuity, holding the Mosaic law fulfilled and replaced by the law of Christ. Dispensationalism and progressive covenantalism sit at various points between. Knowing where a teacher stands on this line tells you a great deal in advance.
